podcast.body: A single from "The Bends" album, notable for its video directed by Jamie Thraves. The video, set near Liverpool Station in London, features a well-dressed man lying on the street, refusing help, and eventually revealing the reason to a gathering crowd, but his words are subtitled and then censored, leading the crowd to also lie down. The band and director have kept the meaning a mystery. The song was a "famous radio hit song" but was "never officially released as a single in North America." "The video for Just was directed by a guy named Jamie Thraves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song originated as a "guitar-shredding competition" between Thom Yorke and Jonny Greenwood, challenging each other to create the most guitar distortion. Years later, Thom Yorke humorously admitted in an interview that Jonny Greenwood was the undisputed winner, acknowledging Greenwood as Radiohead's superior guitarist. "originalmente, hace como una competición de guitarreo entre Tom Jorke y John Gringwood, a ver quién era capaz de distorsionar más la guitarra."

srcs.episode: Cosas que a lo mejor no sabías de THE BENDS

podcast.body: This song, from their 1995 album "The Bends," is famously associated with its music video directed by James Thraves. The video features the band playing in an apartment, while on the street below, a well-dressed man lies down in a fetal position. Subtitles reveal his dialogue with passers-by, stating he's not crazy or drunk, just wants to lie there. Near the end, he reveals his reason, but the subtitles cut out and the editing becomes choppy, making it impossible to discern what he says, even through lip-reading. Whatever he says, it causes everyone on the sidewalk to lie down. The mystery of his words is intentional, designed to leave viewers wondering, similar to the ending of "Lost in Translation." Even the band and video makers claim not to know what the man says. "But near the end of the video, he finally decides to tell everyone why he is actually lying there. However, the subtitles cut out and the editing gets pretty choppy. It's impossible to tell even with lip-reading what this guy says. But whatever he has to say, it has an impact and everybody suddenly lies down on the sidewalk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
